beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: In Jerusalem there was a man who begged at his same spot every day, because he had been sightless from birth. He had never seen his mother's face. Never seen morning. And as Jesus and his disciples passed by, the disciples asked him:

beats.text: Master, who did sin, this man, or his parents, that he was born blind?

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Notice they did not ask whether somebody was at fault. They asked which one. It was the question everyone in that world assumed had an answer.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: It was the standard theology of the day: if you are suffering, somebody must have earned it. People still run that math on themselves today. Jesus threw the whole equation out.

beats.speaker: jesus
beats.text: Neither hath this man sinned, nor his parents: but that the works of God should be made manifest in him.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Nobody's fault. Not a punishment. Jesus refused to explain the man's suffering — and instead announced what it was about to become: a place where God's work would be seen. Then he knelt down, made soft clay with the dust of the ground, and gently spread it over the blind man's eyes with his own hands.

beats.text: And then the trouble started. The neighbors argued about whether he was even the same man. beats.text: He would not argue theology with trained men. He just told them the one thing that had happened to him, and there was nothing they could do with it.
